aggregate-demand-s1.title: Planned spending in Country X at today's price level

table.caption: Planned spending in Country X, billions of dollars, at an unchanged price level (invented data for practice)

aggregate-demand-s2.title: Three news stories from Quillon
aggregate-demand-s2.text:
Quillon is an invented country. In one month its newspapers report three stories:

  1. Home and stock prices in Quillon jump, so households feel richer.
  2. A deep recession hits Quillon's main trading partner, so foreign incomes fall.
  3. Quillon's firms expect sales to boom next year and plan new factories.

Assume nothing else changes, including the price level, unless a question says so.

items.q: Using the table, calculate total planned spending in Country X this year, in billions of dollars, as $C + I + G + (X - M)$.

why.correct: This year: $700 + 150 + 250 + (140 - 100) = 1{,}140$ billion dollars. Net exports enter as exports minus imports.

mistakes.why: You added imports. Imports are spending on goods made abroad, so they are subtracted: use $X - M$.
That is last year's total. The question asks about this year, with investment at 150 and exports at 140.

items.q: Based on the table, what is the overall effect of the two changes on Country X's aggregate demand curve?
options: It shifts left, because investment fell by more than net exports rose
It shifts right, because exports rose while imports stayed the same
It does not shift, because consumption and government spending did not change
It moves along the curve to a lower price level and less output

why.correct: Total planned spending fell from 1,170 to 1,140 billion dollars at the same price level, so AD shifted left.
options: Right: investment fell by 50 and net exports rose by 20, so spending at the same price level fell by 30, a shift left.
Exports did rise by 20, but investment fell by 50 at the same time. Add both changes before deciding.
AD shifts when any component changes at a given price level, not only C or G. Investment and exports changed here.
The price level is unchanged in the table, so this is not a movement along AD. Spending changed for other reasons, which is a shift.

items.q: Which event could explain the change in investment in the table?
options: Households bought fewer new cars and appliances
Firms grew pessimistic about future sales and cut plans for new equipment
Foreign buyers bought more of Country X's goods
The government built fewer roads and bridges

why.correct: Investment (I) is business spending on capital such as equipment and buildings; it falls when firms expect weaker sales.
options: Household purchases of cars and appliances are consumption, which stayed at 700 in the table.
Right: investment is spending on capital goods, and expected sales drive it. Gloomier expectations cut it.
That raises exports, which did rise in the table, but it is not a change in investment.
Public roads are government spending, which stayed at 250.

items.q: Using the table, calculate Country X's net exports this year, in billions of dollars.

why.correct: Net exports $= X - M = 140 - 100 = 40$ billion dollars.

mistakes.why: You added imports to exports. Net exports are exports minus imports.
You subtracted the wrong way round. Net exports are exports minus imports, $X - M$.

items.q: How does story 1 (rising home and stock prices) affect Quillon's aggregate demand?
options: AD shifts left, because households save their gains instead of spending them
There is a movement down along AD, because the price level falls
AD shifts right, because richer households increase consumption at every price level
AD does not change, because stocks are assets and not goods

why.correct: Higher household wealth raises consumption at every price level: AD shifts right.
options: Households feel richer and usually spend more out of their current income, not less.
Home and stock prices are not the price level of goods and services. A change in wealth shifts AD.
Right: higher wealth raises consumption at every price level, so the whole AD curve moves right.
Buying stocks is not counted in GDP, but feeling richer changes how much households spend on goods and services.

items.q: How does story 2 (a recession abroad) affect Quillon's aggregate demand?
options: AD shifts right, because Quillon's imports become cheaper
AD shifts right, because foreign workers move to Quillon
AD is unaffected, because the recession happens in another country
AD shifts left, because foreigners buy fewer of Quillon's exports

why.correct: Exports depend on foreign incomes. When they fall, Quillon's net exports fall and AD shifts left.
options: A recession abroad lowers foreign incomes; the main effect is fewer exports for Quillon, not cheaper imports.
The story is about foreign spending on Quillon's goods. Nothing in it says workers move.
Exports are part of Quillon's AD, so a fall in foreign buying reaches Quillon directly.
Right: lower foreign incomes cut foreign spending on Quillon's goods, so net exports and AD fall.

items.q: Which component of Quillon's aggregate demand changes first because of story 3?
options: Investment
Consumption
Government spending
Net exports

why.correct: Optimistic firms buy more capital goods (factories and equipment), so investment rises and AD shifts right.
options: Right: new factories are capital goods bought by firms, which is investment spending.
Consumption is household spending on goods and services. Factories are bought by firms.
The factories are planned by private firms, not by the government.
Nothing in story 3 is about trade with other countries.

items.q: Considering all three stories together, which statements about Quillon's AD are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Stories 1 and 3 each shift AD to the right
Story 2 shifts AD to the left
The overall direction of the AD shift depends on how large each change is
No story shifts AD, because the price level is unchanged
Story 2 moves Quillon along its AD curve
Story 3 raises AD later, once the factories are finished

why.correct: Stories 1 and 3 push AD right, story 2 pushes it left; with no sizes given, the net direction cannot be told.
options: Right: higher wealth raises C and optimism raises I, both at every price level.
Right: fewer exports lower net exports at every price level.
Right: two forces push right and one pushes left, so the net shift depends on their sizes.
An unchanged price level is exactly why these are shifts: spending changed for reasons other than the price level.
A movement along AD needs a change in the price level. Story 2 changes foreign incomes.
Spending on building the factories is investment the moment it happens; it raises AD right away.

items.q: Which pair of labels belongs on the axes of an aggregate demand graph?
options: Price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis
Price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis
Inflation rate on the vertical axis and unemployment rate on the horizontal axis
Nominal GDP on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis

why.correct: The aggregate demand graph has the price level (PL) on the vertical axis and real GDP (Y) on the horizontal axis.
options: Those are the labels for one market, such as the market for coffee. AD is the whole economy.
Right: AD shows total planned spending on real output at each price level.
Those axes belong to a different graph. AD plots the price level against real GDP.
The vertical axis is a price index for the whole economy, the price level, not nominal GDP.

items.q: The price level falls while household wealth in dollars stays the same. Through the real wealth effect, what happens?
options: Households feel poorer, so consumption falls and AD shifts left
Consumption rises, so the AD curve shifts to the right
The same savings buy more, so consumption rises and real GDP demanded rises along AD
Nothing happens, because wealth measured in dollars did not change

why.correct: The real wealth effect: a lower price level raises the purchasing power of wealth, so real spending rises, a movement down along AD.
options: A lower price level makes the same dollars worth more, so households feel richer, not poorer.
The change starts with the price level, so it is a movement along AD, not a shift of the curve.
Right: a lower price level raises the real value of savings, so households buy more; that is a movement down along AD.
What matters is what the dollars can buy. With lower prices, the same dollars buy more.

items.q: Put the links of the interest rate effect in order, starting from a fall in the price level.
options: The price level falls
People need less money for the same purchases, so they borrow less and lend more
Interest rates fall
Firms and households spend more on investment and big items
Real GDP demanded rises, a movement down along AD

why.correct: With lower prices, less money is needed for the same purchases; more lending and less borrowing lower interest rates, and interest-sensitive spending rises.

items.q: Why does the aggregate demand curve slope down for a different reason than the demand curve for one good?
options: When the price of one good falls, buyers switch to it from other goods, and the same holds for the whole economy
A lower price level raises nominal incomes, so people buy more of everything
Aggregate demand counts government spending, which rises when prices fall
A lower price level changes real wealth, interest rates and the price of a country's goods against foreign goods

why.correct: One good's demand slopes down partly because buyers switch goods. For the whole economy three effects do the work: the real wealth effect, the interest rate effect and the exchange rate effect.
options: Switching between goods explains one market's demand. When the whole price level falls there is no other domestic good to switch from.
A lower price level does not raise nominal incomes; it raises what a given income or savings can buy.
Government spending is set by policy, not by the price level, and it is not why AD slopes down.
Right: AD slopes down because of the real wealth effect, the interest rate effect and the exchange rate effect, which act on the whole economy.

items.q: The price level in Country Z falls while prices abroad stay the same. Through the exchange rate effect, what happens to Country Z's spending?
options: Its goods become cheaper relative to foreign goods, so net exports rise along AD
Its goods become dearer relative to foreign goods, so net exports fall
Imports rise because foreign goods are now cheaper for Country Z
AD shifts right because exports are a component of AD

why.correct: A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods relatively cheaper: exports rise, imports fall, and real GDP demanded rises along AD.
options: Right: exports rise and imports fall, so net exports and real GDP demanded rise, a movement down along AD.
A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods cheaper, not dearer, compared with foreign goods.
Foreign prices did not change while Country Z's fell, so foreign goods are relatively dearer and imports fall.
Exports rise here because Country Z's price level fell, so it is a movement along AD, not a shift.

items.q: Firms become much more optimistic about future sales and raise their spending on new equipment. Shift the aggregate demand curve to show the effect.

why.correct: More investment at every price level shifts AD to the right.

slips.AD: More investment spending raises planned spending at every price level, so AD shifts right.

items.q: Nothing shifts, but the price level falls. Mark a point X on the aggregate demand curve showing the new price level and real GDP demanded.

why.correct: A fall in the price level is a movement down along AD: a lower price level and more real GDP demanded.

items.q: Make it specific: build the chain from a rise in household wealth to aggregate demand.

why.correct: Higher wealth raises consumption at every price level, so AD shifts right.

specific.frame: Household wealth rises, so consumption ___ at every price level; ___ shifts to the ___.
specific.model: When household wealth rises, consumption increases at every price level because households feel richer, so the aggregate demand curve shifts to the right.

spending.label: Consumption
options: rises
falls

why.1: Richer households spend more, not less.

curve.label: The curve
options: aggregate demand
the demand for one good

why.1: Consumption across the whole economy is part of aggregate demand.

direction.label: Which way
options: right
left

why.1: More spending at every price level is a shift right.

items.q: The government cuts income taxes, and households keep more of each paycheck. What happens to aggregate demand?
options: It shifts left, because the government collects less money to spend
It shifts right, because take-home pay and consumption rise
It moves along the curve, because taxes are a kind of price
It shifts right, because the government buys more goods

why.correct: A tax cut raises households' take-home pay, so consumption and AD rise at every price level.
options: A tax cut changes taxes, not the government's spending plans; G is unchanged here.
Right: lower taxes leave households more to spend, so consumption rises at every price level.
Taxes are not the price level. A tax change shifts AD through consumption.
The government did not raise its purchases here; the effect works through households' spending.
